notes.short: “Less than the least,” and grace is lifted up
notes.about: Paul calls himself less than the least of all the saints. He sets himself as low as he can, so that the grace given him, to preach “the unsearchable riches of Christ,” is seen the greater. One writer stresses that he means it: this is true humility, not false modesty.

figure.name: Meiosis
figure.words: less than the least of all the saints
figure.means: Paul sets himself as low as he can, so that the grace given him to preach Christ is seen the greater

original.note: In Paul's Greek “less than the least” is one word, a comparative built on the word for least.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Meiosis (a belittling) and says it marks the apostle's growth in grace. Calvin says Paul shows himself in as humbling a light as possible so that God's grace may be the more exalted, and that he is sincere. Clarke says Paul, aiming to magnify Christ's grace, lays himself as low as possible, even coining a new word for it.
notes.limit: One writer adds that the words show Paul's growth in grace, since later still he calls himself the worst of sinners (1 Timothy 1:15).

cites.quote: “Who am less than the least of all saints.” This marks the apostle’s growth in grace, who a year after could say he was “the chief of sinners”
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: He labors to exhibit himself, and everything that belongs to him, in as humiliating a light as possible, in order that the grace of God may be the more highly exalted. ... This is no hypocritical declaration.

As the design of the apostle was to magnify the grace of Christ in the salvation of the world ... To lay himself as low as possible, consistently with his being in the number of Divinely commissioned men, he calls himself less than the least; and is obliged to make a new word, by strangely forming a comparative degree, not from the positive ... but from the superlative.

notes.short: The believer pictured as a soldier in God's armor
notes.about: Paul carries one picture through seven verses: the believer is a soldier in God's full armor, standing against the devil. Each piece is matched with one thing: truth, righteousness, the gospel of peace, faith, salvation, and the word of God. In 1 Thessalonians 5:8 the picture is brief.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: Put on the full armor of God
figure.means: all that God provides believers to stand against the devil, each piece of armor standing for something such as truth, faith or salvation

original.note: In Paul's Greek “full armor” is panoplia, a soldier's complete armor for defense and attack.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Ephesians 6:11 onward under Allegory. Barnes says the whole description comes from an ancient soldier's weapons; Calvin, that Paul fits a Christian's chief marks to the comparison he began; Clarke, that Paul sees each Christian as a soldier in Greek armor; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown), an image from the Roman armory; Barry (Ellicott), an image worked out in full.
notes.limit: One of the writers warns against pressing why truth, righteousness and the rest are each matched with one piece of armor rather than another.

cites.at: Allegory, or Continued Metaphor and Hypocatastasis, p. 750
cites.quote: For other examples, see Joh 4:35 … Eph 6:11, etc.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The whole description here is derived from the weapons of an ancient soldier. The various parts of those weapons - constituting the "whole panoply" - are specified in Eph 6:14-17. … means "complete armor," offensive and defensive … "The armor of God" is not that which God wears, but that which he has provided for the Christian soldier.

cites.quote: Nothing can be more idle than the extraordinary pains which some have taken to discover the reason why righteousness is made a breastplate, instead of a girdle. Paul’s design was to touch briefly on the most important points required in a Christian, and to adapt them to the comparison which he had already used. Truth, which means sincerity of mind, is compared to a girdle.

The apostle considers every Christian as having a warfare to maintain against numerous, powerful, and subtle foes; and that therefore they would need much strength, much courage, complete armor, and skill to use it. The panoply which is mentioned here refers to the armor of the heavy troops among the Greeks … To all these the apostle refers below.

cites.quote: The panoply offensive and defensive. An image readily suggested by the Roman armory, Paul being now in Rome. … In Rom 13:14 it is, "Put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ"; in putting on Him, and the new man in Him, we put on "the whole armor of God."

cites.quote: He paints the Christian life as a battle against spiritual powers of evil, waged in the strength of the Lord, and in the panoply of God. We trace the germ of this great passage first in St. Paul’s earliest Epistle (1Th 5:8-9) … the image there briefly touched is here worked out in full beauty of detail.
